summary: Menopausal hormone therapy (MHT) alleviates climacteric symptoms, yet its microbiome-wide effects and efficacy determinants remain unclear. Here we show that oral estradiol/dydrogesterone, given for 6 months to 356 perimenopausal women, improved neuroendocrine, metabolic and symptom outcomes and induced site-specific microbial remodeling. Vaginocervical and urinary niches showed the most pronounced restructuring, with moderate oral and minimal gut changes. MHT increased vaginocervical Lactobacillus crispatus and reduced Gardnerella vaginalis. Higher baseline vaginocervical L. crispatus predicted greater postintervention vaginocervical and urinary colonization and superior Female Sexual Function Index improvement. Baseline vaginocervical community types determined differential outcomes: G. vaginalis-dominated individuals shifted most toward healthier communities, whereas diversified individuals improved least. MHT efficacy also varied according to baseline gut community type: Phocaeicola vulgatus-dominated women exhibited greater hormonal responsiveness, superior clinical outcomes and were more likely to achieve 4-week rapid clinical remission than Prevotella copri-dominated women. These findings support a precision MHT framework integrating gut and vaginocervical community typing for personalized care. Chictr.org.cn ID: ChiCTR2100049768 . In this study, the gut, oral, urinary and vaginocervical microbiomes of women receiving menopausal hormone therapy were studied over 6 months, shedding light on how system metagenomics can inform clinical response and care.
title: Heterogeneity of microbiome responses to menopausal hormone therapy among perimenopausal women

summary: Gastrointestinal (GI) microbiome disruption and impaired GI barrier integrity increase the risk of bloodstream infection (BSI) following allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant. Here we report results from a two-cohort (open-label, n = 15; randomized, placebo-controlled, n = 45) phase 1b study of SER-155, an investigational, cultivated, multi-strain, oral live biotherapeutic designed to address GI microbiome disruption GI epithelial barrier integrity in allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant recipients. In cohort 2, 34 of 45 participants received either SER-155 treatment (n = 20, SER-155 following microbiome conditioning with oral vancomycin), or placebo (n = 14), and subsequently received transplant. For the primary safety endpoint, SER-155 was well tolerated, with a safety profile comparable to placebo, no treatment-related serious adverse events and no infections with SER-155 species; the most common adverse events were diarrhea and nausea. Four participants in cohort 1 and four participants in cohort 2 (two participants in the SER-155 arm and two in the placebo arm) died during the study; none was attributable to SER-155. For the primary pharmacokinetic endpoint, engraftment was detected for 16 of 16 SER-155 strains, with a median of 11.5 strains detected after the first treatment course. The key secondary efficacy endpoint revealed a significantly lower incidence of BSI with SER-155 versus placebo (10.0% versus 43%; OR 0.15; 95% CI 0.01–1.13; P = 0.0423; 77% relative risk reduction). Other secondary efficacy endpoints (GI infection, acute graft-versus-host disease ≥grade 2, febrile neutropenia and a composite endpoint of BSI, GI infection or acute graft-versus-host disease) were not statistically significant. The secondary pharmacodynamic endpoint of GI domination by Enterococcus and Enterobacteriaceae spp. was not achieved. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04995653 . In a phase 1b study that included an open-label and randomized-controlled cohorts of allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation recipients, treatment with the investigational, cultivated, multi-strain bacterial oral live biotherapeutic product, SER-155, was found to have a similar safety profile to placebo and resulted in fewer bloodstream infections, indicating further clinical investigation of this therapeutic is warranted.
title: A live biotherapeutic product for adult allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation recipients: a partially randomized, placebo-controlled phase 1b trial

summary: Although highly preventable, cervical cancer remains one of the most common malignancies among women worldwide. As part of the Global Burden of Disease study, we estimated cervical cancer incidence, mortality and disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) across 204 countries and territories from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts to 2050. In 2023, 887,000 new cases (95% uncertainty interval 682,000–1,170,000), 369,000 deaths (292,000–475,000) and 13.3 million DALYs (10.1–17.4) were estimated globally. Age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) and age-standardized mortality rates (ASMR) were more than four and seven times higher in low- versus high-income countries. Between 1990 and 2023, global ASIR was largely stable (−0.4% (–26.6 to 34.7)), whereas ASMR changed by −17.5% (–36.2 to 13.4). All cervical cancer DALYs were attributable to human papillomavirus infection, with tobacco use contributing 5.9% (3.2–9.3) globally. By 2050, global ASIR and ASMR are forecast to change by −12.5% (–25.7 to 3.5) and −9.0% (–21.5 to 6.6) from 2024, yet absolute cases and deaths are forecast to rise by 20.2% (4.6–38.5) and 39.3% (23.6–57.3). ASIR and ASMR are forecast to remain highest in low-income countries. Intensified action is needed to accelerate progress. Analyses of the Global Burden of Disease study reported 887,000 new cases and 369,000 deaths from cervical cancer worldwide in 2023, which are forecasted to rise by 2050.
title: Global, regional and national burden of cervical cancer in 1990–2023 with forecasts to 2050: a Global Burden of Disease study

summary: Preoperative immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) are active in patients with deficient mismatch repair (dMMR) colon cancer (CC), whereas proficient mismatch repair (pMMR) CC has been consistently considered resistant to first-generation ICIs. In the phase 2 UNICORN trial, we evaluated short-course preoperative botensilimab (BOT; multifunctional Fc-enhanced anti-CTLA-4 monoclonal antibody) alone or in combination with the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody balstilimab (BOT + BAL) in 56 patients with resectable, locally advanced CC. Twenty-eight patients with pMMR CC were sequentially enrolled in BOT (n = 14) and BOT + BAL (n = 14) cohorts. Twenty-eight patients with dMMR CC followed the same sequential allocation strategy. The primary endpoint of centrally assessed pathological major response (pMR) rate (≤10% of residual viable tumor) was met in all cohorts, except pMMR BOT. Specifically, the pMR rate was 0% (95% confidence interval (CI): 0−23.2%) in pMMR BOT, 36% (95% CI: 12.8−64.9%) in pMMR BOT + BAL, 36% (95% CI: 12.8−64.9%) in dMMR BOT and 100% (95% CI: 76.8−100%) in dMMR BOT + BAL. Secondary endpoints included safety, quality of life, describing treatment-induced transcriptional dynamics, peripheral blood mononuclear cell dynamics, radiomics and radiogenomics features, fecal microbiota composition and circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) dynamics. Eight (29%) and 15 (54%) patients treated with BOT and BOT + BAL, respectively, experienced immune-related adverse events, most commonly flu-like syndrome and diarrhea. Single-cell spatial transcriptomic analysis of matched baseline and post-treatment samples highlighted high baseline PD-L1 stromal expression and low post-treatment regulatory T cell signatures in pMMR responders, whereas dMMR responders displayed high baseline FCGR2A and FCGR3A expression on intratumoral macrophages. Clearance of ctDNA before surgery correlated with pathological response and lack of recurrence at data cutoff. Preoperative BOT + BAL elicits pathological responses in patients with pMMR or dMMR CC, supporting the combination as a promising strategy to expand ICI benefits to the early-stage setting. ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT05845450 . In the phase 2 UNICORN trial, a short course of neoadjuvant botensilimab and balstilimab achieved the primary endpoint of pathological major response rate in patients with pMMR or dMMR colon cancer.
title: Neoadjuvant botensilimab with or without balstilimab in pMMR and dMMR colon cancer: the phase 2 UNICORN trial

summary: There is an unmet need for repigmentation therapies for patients with nonsegmental vitiligo (NSV) who are candidates for systemic therapy. Here, 52-week primary results are reported from two parallel phase 3, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of once-daily povorcitinib (oral, highly selective JAK1 inhibitor) 30 mg in adults with moderate-to-severe NSV (STOP-V1 and STOP-V2). STOP-V1 and STOP-V2 enrolled 467 and 449 patients, respectively. In both studies, the primary endpoint of ≥75% improvement in the facial Vitiligo Area Scoring Index (F-VASI75) at week 52 was met, demonstrating statistically significant and clinically meaningful repigmentation with povorcitinib versus placebo (STOP-V1: 18.9% versus 6.8%; odds ratio, 3.1; 95% confidence interval 1.6–5.9; P = 0.0003; STOP-V2: 18.9% versus 3.1%; odds ratio, 7.5; 95% confidence interval 3.0–18.6; P < 0.0001). Povorcitinib was well tolerated; the percentage of patients with any treatment-emergent adverse event (TEAE) was similar between the povorcitinib and placebo groups in both studies (STOP-V1/STOP-V2, 68.7%/66.7% versus 63.7%/62.7%). The most common TEAEs with povorcitinib were nasopharyngitis (STOP-V1/STOP-V2, 11.2%/11.3% versus placebo, 9.8%/11.1%), acne (10.7%/10.8% versus 3.0%/2.2%) and upper respiratory tract infection (6.9%/14.0% versus 9.0%/10.7%). Serious TEAEs were generally single events, and Janus kinase inhibitor class-specific TEAEs were absent or rare. These results support once-daily povorcitinib as an effective and well-tolerated systemic treatment for adults with moderate-to-severe NSV. ClinicalTrials.gov identifiers: NCT06113445 , NCT06113471 . In the STOP-V1 and STOP-V2 trials, povorcitinib (an oral JAK1 inhibitor) was superior to placebo in improvement in F-VASI75 score in individuals with nonsegmental vitiligo.
title: Povorcitinib for nonsegmental vitiligo: two randomized, controlled, phase 3 STOP-V trials

summary: Climate change threatens decades of progress toward malaria elimination across the Asia Pacific. In recent years, reported cases have increased sharply in several regions, including Pakistan following the 2022 floods. However, current research and adaptation strategies have largely focused on gradual warming and shifting transmission seasons and may not fully capture acute operational disruptions in endemic settings. Here we examine how climate change influences malaria through cascading disruptions to health systems, population displacement and ecological change. As a multidisciplinary group of policymakers and researchers, we identify priority actions: integrating malaria control into disaster response, deploying adaptive vector control for displaced populations, strengthening cross-border data sharing, linking early warnings to anticipatory action, and incorporating land-use data into surveillance. Leveraging existing advances in climate policy, digital surveillance and community engagement will be critical. Sustaining elimination will require complementing long-term projections with preparedness for near-term system shocks. A multidisciplinary group of policymakers and researchers discusses the impacts of climate change on malaria in the Asia Pacific, identifies gaps in national adaptation strategies and outlines five priority actions for the region.
title: Climate change threatens malaria elimination in the Asia Pacific

summary: Researchers developed a digital twin framework to safely evaluate the effects of drugs on the immune system and time to labor, which could enable personalized interventions to prevent preterm births.
title: Applying digital twins to prevent preterm births

summary: Preclinical analysis and a phase 1 trial support VG-3927 as a promising drug candidate for Alzheimer’s disease, demonstrating successful penetration of the central nervous system, target engagement and tolerability.
title: A small-molecule TREM2 agonist for Alzheimer’s disease
